inputs.original_text: The Punjab and Haryana High Court is right to reject suspicion as a basis for prolonged detention. Alleged phone contact with a Karachi-based “Punjabi Kuri” is not proof, and invoking national security provisions and the Official Secrets Act cannot excuse keeping someone locked up without a case the state can actually establish. Security powers are especially dangerous when they turn suspicion into punishment. Due process and liberty must apply to everyone, and the state—not the accused—must bear the burden of proving its case.
inputs.modified_text: The High Court is right: suspicion is not evidence, and a phone contact with a Karachi-based “Punjabi Kuri” cannot by itself justify prolonged detention. Invoking national security or the Official Secrets Act doesn’t make it acceptable to lock someone up when the state cannot establish a case. These powers can turn fear into punishment, with the accused forced to bear the cost of the state’s failure to prove its claims. Due process and liberty must protect everyone.
